morningLine: The graphical future gets a cheaper price tag, and the home-computer aisle gains a formidable new package.

lead.headline: Apple Slashes Lisa by $3,000 as Sculley Resets the Company
lead.dek: A stripped-down $6,995 configuration aims to revive the pioneering graphical workstation while IBM seizes the middle of the personal-computer market.
body: Apple Computer opened the week with a dramatic answer to sluggish Lisa sales: dealers were told that the $9,995 mouse-driven workstation would be offered in a stripped-down $6,995 configuration. The $3,000 cut followed new president John Sculley’s four-day tour addressing some 1,500 dealers in 25 cities, a public show of urgency from a company suddenly chasing IBM in the market it helped create.

Lisa’s graphical desktop and integrated office applications still looked like a preview of personal computing’s future, but the machine’s price kept it beyond many offices. Time reported that only about 6,000 units had sold and quoted a Crocker National Bank executive saying even $5,000 might only make the bank interested, not convinced. Apple was also preparing IBM PC program compatibility for Lisa, an acknowledgment that corporate buyers increasingly expected access to IBM’s software world.

The competitive arithmetic had changed quickly. Dataquest figures cited in the period press put IBM at 28 percent of the $1,000-to-$5,000 computer segment, up from 12 percent the previous December, while Apple held 21 percent. The Apple IIe remained a brisk seller and cost roughly $1,500 less than an IBM PC, but dealers were already bracing for IBM’s rumored lower-cost “Peanut” machine.

Behind the Lisa maneuver stood a smaller gamble. Contemporary reporting said Apple planned a January 18 introduction for Macintosh at about $2,500, carrying Lisa-derived ideas into a more accessible computer, though with less storage and no initial compatibility with Lisa or IBM PC programs. By Friday, Apple warned that quarterly earnings would fall sharply; its shares, once $63.25 in June, closed the week near $29.38. The company’s graphical vision was intact, but the market was demanding a far cheaper way to buy it.

stories.headline: FCC Clears Coleco’s Adam for the Holiday Computer Battle
stories.dek: The approximately $700 all-in-one package can finally head for stores with 64K, data drive, printer, and ColecoVision compatibility.
body: Coleco said Thursday that federal regulators had cleared Adam for sale, removing the last formal obstacle between the ambitious home-computer package and Christmas shoppers. The company expected the machine to reach stores for the holiday season, where its promised combination of computer, storage, printer, and videogame compatibility would be measured against Commodore and Atari.

The complete package was announced at about $700, with 64K of user memory, a proprietary Digital Data Pack drive, and a daisy-wheel printer. Adam could run ColecoVision cartridges, while an expansion version was intended for people who already owned the console. Earlier in September, Coleco and AT&T had also announced plans for home-computer and videogame services delivered over telephone lines, giving Adam a communications story as well as a game library.

stories.headline: Portable Computers Crowd the Road-Warrior Market
stories.dek: September’s machines range from suitcase-like CP/M systems to battery-minded lap-size designs.
body: BYTE devoted its September cover package to “Portable Computers in Depth,” evidence that portability had become a category rather than a novelty. Buyers could choose integrated screens, disk drives, and bundled business programs, but every design negotiated the same hard tradeoffs: weight, battery life, display size, storage, and price.

The familiar Osborne and Kaypro approach put a complete CP/M office into a case a determined traveler could carry. Newer battery-oriented machines pointed toward something closer to a briefcase companion. Period reviews and advertisements show a market experimenting in public, with no settled answer yet to what a portable computer ought to be.

stories.headline: IBM’s Shadow Lengthens Across Personal Computing
stories.dek: Apple’s price move comes as IBM leads the key mid-price segment and dealers await a cheaper home machine.
body: IBM’s rise now shapes nearly every decision in the personal-computer business. Dataquest estimates placed Big Blue at 28 percent of the $1,000-to-$5,000 segment, ahead of Apple’s 21 percent, a reversal achieved in less than two years.

Apple still had the popular IIe and was developing a simpler, lower-cost version, but compatibility had become a decisive sales argument. Reports of IBM’s cheaper “Peanut,” expected in October, threatened to carry the company’s name from the office into the family room. It would emerge as the PCjr, but this week dealers knew it only as the next pressure point.
